uncited: This family encompasses techniques for rendering volumetric datasets that exceed the memory or processing capacity of a single machine by distributing the workload across multiple nodes or processes [S1][S2, S4, unofficial].
It solves the scalability bottleneck inherent in single-node rendering by partitioning data or computation [S1][S2, unofficial].
**Decomposition:** The input volume or mesh is partitioned into subsets.
This can be spatial (sub-volumes) or topological (mesh cells) [S1][S2, S4, unofficial].
**Distribution:** Subsets are assigned to distinct processing units (MPI ranks, cluster nodes) [S1][S2, S4, unofficial].
**Local Rendering:** Each unit renders its assigned subset independently, typically using ray casting or projection [S1][S2, S4, unofficial].
**Compositing/Assembly:** Results from all units are combined to form the final image.
This occurs either via pixel-based accumulation over the network (e.g., SDVR) or image-based assembly by a root process (e.g., MPI 1D/2D) [S1][S2, S4, unofficial].

Distributed volume rendering emerged in the late 1990s and early 2000s as a response to the growing size of scientific datasets (e.g., CFD, medical imaging) exceeding single-processor capabilities [S1][S2, S4, unofficial].

Early work focused on MPI-based decomposition of structured grids [S1, S2, S4, unofficial], while later approaches addressed unstructured meshes using graph partitioning or round-robin strategies to handle irregular computational costs [S1, unofficial][S2].
